volume 16,  Article number: 29358 (2026) Cite this article The adsorption of V-series nerve agents (VE, VG, VM, VX) on graphene oxide (GO) was systematically investigated using density functional theory (DFT) at the ωB97X-D/6-311G(d, p) level. Basis set superposition error (BSSE)-corrected adsorption energies reveal that physisorption governs the interaction, with the strongest binding observed for the GO Mid-COH/VG(O112) configuration at − 1.120 eV. The mid-sheet hydroxyl group consistently outperformed the terminal carboxyl group as the primary binding site. Validated theoretical IR and Raman spectra versus experimental ones accurately reproduced characteristic GO bands, and provided sage and reliable vibrational fingerprints for the V-agents, noting a P–S stretch shift from 617 cm⁻¹ (VG) to 521 cm⁻¹ (VX). Frontier molecular orbital analysis confirmed that the GO HOMO-LUMO gap remains stable (~ 5.1 eV), verifying non-covalent interactions. Population analysis identified V-agents as electron donors, where VX exhibited the highest charge transfer (ΔN = − 0.106) and lowest reorganization energy (\({{\uplambda}}_{hole}\) = 0.651 eV) among the studied agents. Molecular electrostatic potential and Electron Localization Function analyses confirmed that hydrogen bonding at the P=O group drives the physisorption mechanism. Ultimately, the consistent adsorption behavior and pronounced dipole moment alterations establish GO as a theoretically promising platform for the capture and electrical detection of V series nerve agents, warranting further experimental investigation. Nerve agents are a class of highly toxic chemicals that disrupt the normal functioning of the nervous system1. They are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which is they enzyme that breaks down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. This inhibition causes increase in the level of acetylcholine, thus resulting in overstimulation of muscles, glands, and the central nervous system2. Nerve agents are extremely poisonous, and even small amounts can cause severe health effects. Symptoms can appear rapidly after exposure, and the common symptoms of exposure to nerve agents include miosis (constricted pupils), rhinorrhea (runny nose), coughing and breathing difficulties, loss of consciousness, seizures and paralysis, and even death if not treated promptly3. They can be absorbed through inhalation, ingestion, or skin contact and even a tiny amount can be lethal, making them particularly dangerous in chemical warfare or terrorist attacks4. Immediate treatment is crucial and typically involves the administration of antidotes such as atropine and pralidoxime, along with supportive care to manage symptoms5. Some well-known nerve agents include sarin, tabun, and v-series nerve agents, each of which has specific characteristics and methods of delivery6. The V-series nerve agents are a group of highly toxic organophosphate chemical warfare agents (CWAs) known for their potency and lethality7. The “V” stands for “venomous,” and these agents are characterized by their ability to inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine, which in turn overstimulates the nervous system8. VX is the most famous and widely recognized of the V-series, and is an extremely potent nerve agent that is tasteless and odorless amber-colored, oily liquid, and can be absorbed through the skin, inhaled, or ingested9. VM, VG and VE are also highly potent nerve agents that, similar to VX, function primarily as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors10,11. V-series nerve agents generally exhibit higher toxicity than G-series nerve agents (like sarin and tabun) and can be effective in much smaller quantities, and are better absorbed through the skin compared to G-series agents, increasing the risk of exposure in a chemical attack12. Consequently, there is a need for the design and production of sustainable and stable chemical sensors with superior performance in terms of reaction time and sensitivity. Gas sensors detect the presence of gases and quantify their concentration in the environment. These sensors are used in various applications, including industrial safety, environmental monitoring, and indoor air quality assessment13. Gas sensors can be designed to detect specific gases or a range of gases, and they operate based on different principles14. Electrochemical gas sensors detect gases through chemical reactions that produce a measurable electrical current. They are commonly used for detecting toxic gases like carbon monoxide (CO) and hydrogen sulfide (H2S)15. Infrared gas sensors detect gases by measuring the absorption of infrared light at specific wavelengths. They are more commonly applied for sensing gases like carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4)16. Semiconductor gas sensors use a semiconductor material that operates via the change in its electrical resistance in response to detecting certain gases. They are often employed to detect volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and other gases17. Photoionization detectors (PIDs) represent another glass of gas sensors that employ a high-power lamp to ionize gas molecules, allowing for the detection of a wide range of gases, especially VOCs18. Catalytic gas sensors are capable of detecting combustible gases by measuring changes in temperature when the gas is burned on a catalyst. They are commonly used for the detection of propane and natural gas19. Metal-oxide gas sensors detect gases by measuring changes in conductivity in a metal-oxide material when exposed to specific gases, such as ammonia and hydrogen20. Some previous studies introduced sensors for nerve agents. The study by Marlar and Harb21 introduced an electrochemical sensor based on Zr-based metal-organic framework (MOF), MOF-808 for detecting demeton-S-methylsulfon as a VX simulant. Fan et al.8 introduced a fluorescence-based method to rapidly differentiate between the V-series and G-series nerve agents where VX and the less toxic simulant VO were detected using photoinduced hole transfer. Puglisi et al.22 reported on smartphone portable detection system based on multiple hydrogen-bond interactions for the sensing of sub-ppm levels of dimethyl methylphosphonate as a nerve agent simulant in the gas phase. Banerjee et al.23 synthesized and characterized a probe based on the methoxy naphthalene-furoic hydrazide group for rapid detection and quantification of diethyl chlorophosphate nerve agent. Park et al.24 designed Au (III) coordinated polymeric films for the detection of the VX simulant demeton-S. Zappalà et al.25 developed surface-enhanced Raman scattering substrates from Si-based Au nanoparticles for the detection of Tabun and VX nerve agents. Graphene oxide (GO) is a single-atomic layered material derived from graphite, arranged in a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice, and characterized by the presence of various oxygen-containing functional groups such as epoxy, hydroxyl and carboxyl groups26. This structure gives GO unique properties that make it suitable for a wide range of applications. It exhibits high tensile strength and flexibility, making it a strong candidate for composite materials27. Depending on its degree of oxidation, GO can also behave as a semiconductor or insulator, which allows for tunable electronic properties by controlling the ratio of sp2 and sp3 hybridized carbon28. GO also has excellent thermal conductivity and high optical transparency, making it useful in heat management applications and transparent conductive films29. GO, like other graphene derivatives and carbon-based systems, was implemented in the production of electrochemical gas sensors to detect water vapor, heptane and ethyl acetate30, ethanol, acetone and ethylbenzene31, CO2, NO2, and H2S32, and CO33. Molecular modeling using Density Functional Theory (DFT) is a powerful computational technique used to investigate the electronic structure of molecules and materials34. DFT allows the calculation of different properties such as molecular geometries, energies, and reaction pathways with a balance of accuracy and computational efficiency35. Consequently, molecular modeling is considered a very useful and efficient tool in studying physical and spectroscopic properties of V-series nerve agents, as well as their interactions with other materials, since their highly toxic nature makes them extremely difficult to be handled experimentally. DFT calculations at M05-2X/6–31++G(d, p) level of theory were conducted to study the adsorption of VR and A-series nerve agents on 2-D carbon nitride (C2N) surface as an electrochemical sensor36. Using the same level of theory, DFT investigation of C2N quantum dots was also performed as an electrochemical sensor for V-series nerve agents37. Different DFT functionals with the same basis set of 6–311++G(d, p) were employed in studying the hydrolysis rate of A-, V-, and G-series nerve agents38. DFT with B3LYP and M06-2X hybrid exchange-correlation functionals were used to study the electronic and spectroscopic properties of A-series and V-series nerve agents39. From GO’s point of view as an adsorbent, a number of experimental and computational contributions have already examined the interaction of organophosphate compounds with graphene-based substrates. For example, the interlayer spacing of graphene oxide frameworks has been tuned to enhance the diffusion and detection of the simulant dimethyl methylphosphonate (DMMP)40, while DFT calculations have been used to assess the sensing response of GO toward volatile industrial compounds such as phosgene and HCl41. Separately, carbon nanocones have been proposed as potential traps for VX and Novichok based on combined DFT and molecular dynamics simulations42. A recent combined experimental and computational study on molybdenum iodide cluster supported on graphene (Mo6@Graphene) demonstrated fast and sensitive detection of DMMP simulant with a limit of detection of 270 ppb, where DFT calculations identified H-bonding interactions as the sensing mechanism, though this study is limited to a simulant rather than actual nerve agents43. A first-principles DFT study on pristine graphene nanoribbons demonstrated their potential for sarin nerve gas sensing, through analysis of structural, electronic and transport properties, though the study is limited to band structure and density of states analysis, with no adsorption energy calculations, BSSE correction, dispersion correction, frequency validation, or charge transfer quantification44. Another experimental investigation of 3D graphene/carbon nanotube composite for DMMP adsorption showed improved breakthrough time and dynamic adsorption capacity by 33.5% and 39%, respectively, compared to commercial activated carbon45. These efforts collectively highlight the promise of carbonaceous materials for chemical defense applications. Yet, direct DFT-level studies of actual V-series agents on the intrinsic, oxygen-rich surface of graphene oxide remain scarce, particularly those that incorporate explicit spectroscopic validation. The above-mentioned works either rely on simulants, use modified frameworks or alternative morphologies, or focus primarily on macroscopic diffusion and capacitance rather than on the local electronic structure of the adsorbed complex. In this context, the present study examines the adsorption of V-series agents (VE, VG, VM, VX) on pristine GO using rigorous and comprehensive first-principles DFT protocol that combines calculated IR and Raman spectra against experimental benchmarks, along with frontier molecular orbital analysis, two complementary charge-transfer quantification methods (Pearson and ADCH), and Electron Localization Function (ELF) visualization. The study moves beyond mere adsorption energy calculations to provide a multi-faceted electronic-level understanding. The aim is to elucidate the nature of the interactions (physisorption versus chemisorption), quantify charge transfer, identify the most reactive sites on both the adsorbent and adsorbates, and ultimately establish a structure-activity relationship that predicts the efficacy of GO for the capture and detection of these extremely toxic compounds. This combination does not claim to supersede previous findings; rather, it provides a fundamental electronic-level foundation that can inform the rational design of GO-based materials for the capture and detection of these extremely toxic compounds. GO was prepared using modified Hummer’s method described by Elhaes et al.46. Briefly, in a 9:1 ratio, H2SO4 and H3PO4 were combined, then 1 g of graphite powder was combined with 6 g of KMnO4 in an ice bath. The two solutions were then mixed followed by agitated for 12 h at 50 C. The resulting solution was cooled then transferred into 1 mL of 30% H2O2 ice. The solution was then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm to collect the precipitate. The precipitate was first washed using 200 mL of 30% HCl, then was washed multiple times by deionized water, and finally left to dry overnight in a room temperature-vacuum oven. FTIR spectrum of GO was obtained using VERTEX 80v FTIR spectrometer (Bruker Optik GmbH, Germany) using the KBr pellet method. The FTIR absorbance spectrum was acquired in the spectral range of 4000–400 cm−1 with the resolution of 4 cm−1. Raman spectrum of GO was acquired using WITec Alpha300 R confocal Raman microscope (Germany), equipped with a 785 nm laser with the maximum power of 20 mW. The spectrum was recorded over the spectral range of 1800–800 cm−1 using the spectral resolution of 2 cm−1 of Raman shift. The spectrum was taken with 20 s exposure and 30 mW laser power output. All the studied models were subjected to quantum mechanical calculations using GAUSSIAN 09 software47 at Molecular Modeling and Spectroscopy Laboratory, Centre of Excellence for Advanced Science, National Research Centre, Egypt. The geometry of all isolated molecules and the resulting adsorption complexes was fully optimized in the gas phase using the B3LYP functional48,50,50 in conjunction with the 6-31G(d, p) basis set, as the primary aim of this study is to elucidate the intrinsic electronic and bonding properties of the adsorption complexes without the complicating effects of solvation. This level of theory provides an excellent balance between computational cost and accuracy for obtaining reliable molecular structures51. To obtain more accurate energies and electronic properties that are crucial for calculating adsorption energies and analyzing non-covalent interactions, single-point energy calculations were performed on the optimized geometries. These calculations employed the ωB97X-D functional52 and the larger 6-311G(d, p) basis set. The ωB97X-D functional is a range-separated version of Becke’s 97 functional with an added dispersion correction, which is essential for accurately describing the long-range van der Waals forces and dispersion interactions that are paramount in physisorption processes53. Different studies reported the ωB97X-D functional to be the most suitable choice for determining reliable interaction energies and thermodynamic properties, and it performs exceptionally well for non-bonded interactions, clearly outperforming many other long-range corrected functionals. The combination of ωB97X-D with the 6-311G(d, p) basis set gives an accurate description of dispersion forces without the common problem of over-delocalizing electron density. This makes it particularly good at capturing the behavior of gas-phase conformers and intermolecular potentials. This level of theory also offers a good balance, producing high-quality equilibrium structures without introducing artificial stabilization, and despite its accuracy, the method remains computationally manageable, with reasonable SCF convergence times and modest CPU demands, offering a solid compromise between precision and practical efficiency54,56,56. All analyzed properties, including adsorption energy, dipole moment, frontier molecular orbital energies (HOMO-LUMO gap), global reactivity descriptors, charge transfer (Atomic Dipole Corrected Hirshfeld (ADCH)), reorganization energy, molecular electrostatic potential (MEP) maps, projected density of states (PDOS), and Electron Localization Function (ELF) plots, were derived from the ωB97XD/6-311G(d, p) level of theory on the optimized B3LYP/6-31G(d, p) structures. Later on, additional full geometry optimization at ωB97X-D/6-31G(d, p) level was performed for the most stable configurations to verify the structures are not significantly affected by the choice of functional. Theoretical IR and Raman spectra were calculated to confirm that the optimized geometry of the GO model corresponds to a true minimum on the potential energy surface34 and to enable direct comparison with experimental spectra for model validation. To improve the quantitative agreement, the calculated harmonic vibrational wavenumbers were scaled by a factor of 0.9657,58 to account for anharmonicity and known systematic errors of the computational method59,60. This specific scaling factor is highly consistent with well-established benchmark evaluations for long-range corrected hybrid density functionals like ωB97X-D paired with triple-zeta basis sets like 6-311G(d, p)61,62. While mode-specific scaling factors can provide finer corrections for individual vibrational modes, uniform scaling remains a standard, widely accepted approach for improving the agreement between theoretical and experimental spectra. The excellent agreement between our scaled theoretical spectra and the experimental data for the characteristic D and G bands (showing minor deviations of only + 18 and − 19 cm−1, respectively) confirms the empirical suitability of this scaling factor for the present system. PDOS plots were generated using GaussSum software63. ADCH charge transfer was computed, and ELF plots were generated using Multiwfn 3.8 software64,65. The Basis Set Superposition Error (BSSE) was corrected for using the Counterpoise method (counterpoise = 2 command) to eliminate the artificial lowering of energy caused by the use of the basis set of the adjacent fragment, thereby obtaining physically meaningful and accurate adsorption energies. To assess the influence of environmental conditions on the adsorption process, single-point energy calculations were performed in the presence of water as a solvent using the Polarizable Continuum Model (PCM) as implemented in Gaussian 09. These calculations were carried out at the same level of theory (ωB97X-D/6-311G(d, p)). The PCM approach treats the solvent as a continuous dielectric medium, which provides a reasonable description of the bulk solvation effects without the computational cost of explicit solvent molecules. The solvent effect was monitored by comparing key parameters between the gas-phase and solvated systems, including adsorption energies, dipole moments, HOMO-LUMO gaps, and global reactivity descriptors. A GO sheet containing 3 hydroxyl, 3 epoxy, and 2 carboxyl groups, and VE, VG, VM and VX model molecules were designed using GaussView 5.0 software66. The GO model employed in this study contains a finite cluster of carbon atoms with a limited number of oxygen-containing functional groups. This cluster size is consistent with previous DFT studies of adsorption on GO. Edge effects were minimized by saturating the peripheral carbon atoms with hydrogen atoms. It must be noted that while larger clusters would provide a more complete representation of the GO surface, their use would be computationally prohibitive for the comprehensive analyses performed here. The good agreement between theoretical and experimental IR and Raman spectra provides a strong validation that the model captures the essential structural and vibrational features of GO. The interaction of V-series nerve agents with GO was proposed to take place via hydrogen bonding once with a middle hydroxyl (mid OH) group (OH group composed of atoms O6 and H87) and once with a terminal carboxyl (Ter COOH) group (COOH group composed of atoms C77, O8, O9 and H106). Then, each of VE, VM and VX molecules were proposed to interact with each of the two proposed interaction sites on GO sheet twice through their oxygen atoms, giving a total of 4 proposed interactions for each molecule, since each molecule contains 2 oxygen atoms in its structure. Whereas, VG was proposed to interact three times with each of the two proposed interaction sites on GO sheet giving a total of 6 proposed GO-VG interactions since VG molecule contains 3 oxygen atoms in its structure. VE is proposed to interact through its atoms O110 and O111. VM is proposed to interact through its atoms O109 and O110. VX is proposed to interact through its atoms O110 and O111. VG is proposed to interact through its atoms O110, O111 and O112. The molecules underwent geometry optimization, followed by calculation of the vibrational frequencies to confirm that the optimized structures are representing true minima, through the absence of imaginary frequencies40. Global reactivity descriptors (GRDs) are quantitative measures that characterize the reactivity of molecules. They provide insights into how molecules interact with one another, predict their stability, and assess their reactivity in chemical processes94. These descriptors comprise ionization potential (I), electron affinity (A) chemical potential (µ), electrophilicity index (ω), global hardness (η), global softness (S), and electronegativity (χ)95. Ionization potential and electron affinity are calculated by Koopmans’ theorem96, with ionization potential representing the energy required to remove an electron from the HOMO orbital, and electron affinity representing as the amount of energy released following the addition of an electron to the LUMO orbital97. Chemical potential represents the tendency of a molecule to exchange electrons; hence, it measures the stability of a system; such that molecules with a high chemical potential are more reactive98. Global hardness measures a molecule’s resistance to changes in its electron density; such that a higher global hardness indicates that a molecule is less reactive, while a lower value suggests greater reactivity99. Global softness is the inverse of hardness and indicates how easily a molecule can accept additional electrons, where higher softness value typically correlates with increased reactivity99. Electrophilicity index is the descriptor that quantifies the molecule’s ability to accept electrons, meaning that a higher electrophilicity index suggests that a molecule is a stronger electrophile, thus more likely to react with nucleophiles97. Electronegativity represents the atom’s ability to attract electrons100. Electron Localization Function (ELF) analysis provides a direct visual means of distinguishing between covalent and non-covalent interactions by mapping regions of space where electrons are paired118. In a covalent bond, a continuous region of high ELF (red) bridges the two atoms, indicating shared electron density. In a non-covalent interaction, the electron localization domains of the two fragments remain separate, with a region of low ELF (blue) between them. In addition, hydrogen bonding is typically marked by localized ELF basins around the hydrogen atom of the donor and the acceptor atom, but with a clear gap separating them119. The ELF plots for the two representative configurations – the strongest binding (Mid-COH/VG-O112) and the weakest binding (Ter-COOH/VX-O110) – are shown in Fig. 11, with the remaining configurations provided in Fig. S13–S16 of supplementary materials. Localized basins are present around the hydrogen atom of the GO functional group and the oxygen atom of the nerve agent’s phosphonate moiety, consistent with hydrogen bond formation. With adsorption energies of − 0.385 to − 1.120 eV, desorption should be feasible and the response reversible. Taken together, the results presented above demonstrate a consistent picture of how GO might function as a sensor for V-series agents. The adsorption energies, which range from − 0.385 to − 1.120 eV, indicate a thermodynamically favorable but reversible interaction, which is a useful feature for sensor regeneration. The large changes in dipole moment observed upon adsorption, reaching up to 8.844 Debye, point towards the possibility of electrical detection, as such changes could translate into measurable shifts in conductivity or capacitance. Importantly, the HOMO–LUMO gap of GO remains practically unchanged (≈ 5.1 eV), indicating that the electronic structure of GO remains is not fundamentally altered by the adsorption of the V-series nerve agents, thus suggesting a reversible and reproducible sensing signal. The charge transfer analysis identifies the direction and magnitude of electron flow between the nerve agents and GO’s surface, which is essential for understanding the mechanism of electrical signal generation. Finally, the ELF analysis offers direct visual evidence that the interaction is non-covalent and therefore reversible in nature. We recognize that selectivity against common atmospheric interferents such as water vapor, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen oxides is an important aspect of sensor performance that has not been addressed here. The present study, however, provides a fundamental electronic level understanding of the interaction between GO and V series agents. The adsorption energies, charge transfer fractions, and dipole moment changes all differ noticeably from one agent to another. This suggests that GO may have an inherent preference for certain agents over others, which can inform the rational design of GO based sensors. Future studies should investigate the competitive adsorption of common interferents to assess the selectivity of GO for V-series agents. Additionally, the incorporation of functionalization or doping strategies could enhance selectivity towards specific targets. The theoretical framework established here provides a solid foundation for such future investigations. This study presents a comprehensive DFT investigation into the adsorption of V-series nerve agents on graphene oxide, providing a detailed understanding of the energetic, electronic, spectroscopic and bonding properties governing the interaction. The adsorption energies, corrected for BSSE, confirmed that physisorption is the dominant mechanism, with the Mid-COH/VG(O112) configuration exhibiting the strongest binding at − 1.120 eV. The mid-sheet hydroxyl group consistently outperformed the terminal carboxyl group as the binding site, and a clear inverse relationship between adsorption energy and bond length was established across all configurations. The validation of the computational model through comparison with experimental IR and Raman spectra of GO demonstrated excellent agreement, particularly for the characteristic D and G bands and the fingerprint C–O and C=C regions, confirming the reliability of the theoretical approach. The theoretical IR spectra of the isolated V-agents provided a safe and reliable set of vibrational fingerprints, with the P–S stretch showing a systematic shift that reflects the sensitivity of vibrational spectroscopy to subtle structural differences among these compounds. Electronic structure analysis revealed that the HOMO-LUMO gap of GO remains nearly unchanged upon adsorption (≈ 5.1 eV), confirming the absence of covalent bond formation. Charge transfer analysis using Pearson’s method and ADCH population analysis consistently identified the V-agents as electron donors to the GO surface, with VX exhibiting the highest charge-transfer fraction and lowest reorganization energy, indicating its superior electron-donating ability. The significant changes in dipole moment upon adsorption, particularly the large increases observed for specific configurations such as GO Ter-COOH/VM(O109) (8.844 D), suggest that the adsorption event could be detected by monitoring the resulting electrical signal, making GO a promising platform for the electrical detection of V-series agents. Electrostatic potential mapping identified the oxygen atoms of the phosphonate ester moiety, particularly the P=O group, as the primary nucleophilic sites responsible for hydrogen bonding with the GO surface. Electron Localization Function analysis provided a strong visual confirmation of physisorption, with clearly separated electron localization domains and low-ELF gaps at the interface. The consistency of the ELF topology across all configurations confirms that the interaction mechanism is universal, regardless of the nerve agent or the specific GO functional group involved. In summary, this work demonstrates that graphene oxide is a thermodynamically favorable and electronically responsive material for the capture of V-series nerve agents via a non-covalent physisorption mechanism. The combination of spectroscopic validation, electronic structure analysis and charge transfer characterization provides a solid foundation for the rational design of GO-based sensors and protective materials for chemical defense applications, but experimental verification of the sensing performance is necessary before practical implementation. title: Honda CR-V Driver Claims He Caught a Dealership in a "Lie" After He Took It for an Oil Change - Yahoo Autos
content: A TikTok mechanic said a customer took his Honda CR-V to a dealership and then claims he was told a lie after it claimed that his SUV was leaking. The story adds fuel to the fire that many believe they are being scammed by dealerships. In a viral video viewed over 250,000 times, TikTok user Sean Brown (@talkingshop716), who is also a mechanic, said a customer had taken a Honda CR-V to a dealership for an oil change. Since he had an oil change coupon and the location was convenient, he felt this was the best thing to do. Brown then said the mechanic at the dealership came out to the customer and told them the car was a mess. They described oil everywhere underneath the car and said they needed a new oil pan for the Honda. The customer, however, wasn't convinced that this was correct. So he turned to Brown to get a second opinion on what the dealership had told him. This is what led Brown to claim that he thought the dealership was being dishonest about the situation. Brown said that the customer had gone to a local dealership for an oil change and had done so because it was convenient. Brown also said the customer had an oil change coupon, so it made sense for him to go and get the work done at the dealership. It was then that they came out with a whole host of problems for the owner. "They come out to this customer and say, 'Sir, the underside of your engine is completely covered in oil. Your oil pan is leaking. You've got oil everywhere. We need to replace your oil pan,'" said Brown. The customer was quite concerned and wasn't sure what to believe. So, he decided to get in touch with Brown and find out if the dealership had been correct in its assessment. Brown got the car into his workshop and went to have a look at it. He determined that, as best as he could tell, there was nothing wrong with the car. None of the parts that would have been covered in oil thanks to a leaking oil pan were oil-free, and it looked absolutely fine. Brown also denied that the dealership might have cleaned the oil off. "Unfortunately, I don't think there's a flat-rate mechanic left in this trade outside of some good people that I know that would actually clean that off for a customer after they deny the repair," he said. According to the mechanic, there was nothing wrong at all with the Honda. "You can only lie to people for so long. You're gonna lose all your business," said Brown. He deduced that the dealership had tried to scam the Honda owner and portray any potential problem as far more serious than it actually was. This owner would not be the first to be scammed. Scams like this are common in the industry. Many have said that they are offered free or discounted work, such as an oil change, and are then told that other work is required, meaning a cheap oil change becomes something very expensive. In 2009, investigators in California found 22 locations where a scam of this nature had taken place following 30 undercover visits. In total, there were more than 35 incidents in which car owners were told they needed more work when, in reality, nothing was wrong. And the automaker isn’t shying away from calling out the competition on the other side of Detroit. The arms race between heavy-duty pickup-truck makers is alive and well, even as much of the auto industry focuses on electrifying its lineups. Still, Detroit’s Big Three continue to push the limits of combustion engines, especially with their biggest trucks, and General Motors has just upped the ante one more time. In a new YouTube video, GM just announced a new Duramax diesel 8.3-liter V-8 engine bound for its heavy-duty pickups. Aside from the displacement, we don’t have any engine specs yet. Still, we can be sure that the Mongoose is riddled with superlatives. There’s the name itself: Mongoose, which is a clear shot at Ford’s “Scorpion” 6.7-liter Power Stroke diesel, which powers the brand’s heavy-duty trucks. And then there’s the video, which shows a bow-tie-eyed Mongoose attacking and killing a Scorpion that just so happened to be walking in an oval. So while we don’t know the high end of the Mongoose’s stats, we can be sure of the low end. Considering that the Power Stroke generates 500 horsepower and 1200 pound-feet of torque, the Mongoose is sure to outdo those figures. When it arrives with the 2027 Chevy Silverado HD and 2027 GMC Sierra HD lineups, the Mongoose will supplant GM’s current Duramax 6.6-liter V-8, which churns out 470 horsepower and 975 pound-feet of torque. Those might be respectable figures, but in the world of HD trucks, no one wants to be outdone by their rivals. title: Why no dipstick is needed to check oil in GM's next-gen pickup engines - freep.com
content: General Motors’ next generation pickup trucks mark the next evolution in the automaker’s software-driven vehicle strategy, featuring all-new software systems in the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado and 2027 GMC Sierra that include promises of continued refinement through over-the-air updates. That technological shift even applies to its engines, as the sixth generation V-8 in those 2027 model year trucks will be the first to come without traditional dipsticks to monitor oil levels. GM spokesman Trevor Thompkins confirmed to the Detroit Free Press that a simplified ownership experience drove the decision to switch to electronic oil-level monitoring for the new light-duty 5.7 liter and 6.6 liter V-8 engines. Without cracking the hood, customers can check engine-oil levels from the vehicle cabin through an on-screen readout. “The virtual display continuously monitors oil level, reduces the potential for human error, and can alert drivers when oil levels are too low and how much to add or too high — something a traditional dipstick cannot do,” Thompkins said. There are other benefits to using software over setting reminders to check oil levels. Traditional or virtual dipsticks lack the real-time oil life monitors that GM offers across vehicle nameplates that notify customers when it’s time to change their oil. The 5.7 liter and 6.6 liter V-8s in the model year 2027 Silverado and Sierra are the first and only GM engines using a virtual dipstick, he said. Mark Dickens, executive chief engineer of GM’s full-size trucks and SUVs, noted in a media event on Sept. 16 in Flint that the new lubrication system for the sixth generation V-8’s support the durability and performance efficiency across the ownership cycle. Meanwhile, the LS6 6.7 liter V-8 inside the 2027 Corvette Stingray, Grand Sport and Grand Sport X, still come with oil level dipsticks, as do the other two engines GM unveiled for pickup trucks, the enhanced TurboMax engine and the Duramax 3.0 liter Turbo-Diesel. Among the Detroit Three, or the broader industry, GM is not the first to remove the dipstick. Vehicles equipped with the twin turbo Hurricane six-cylinder engine, which launched in 2023 without a dipstick, include the Jeep Grand Wagoneer, Ram 1500s and the Dodge Charger. title: Phonorecords V Dispute Intensifies as CRB Seeks Additional Info - digitalmusicnews.com
content: Washington, D.C.’s James Madison Memorial Building, which houses the U.S. Copyright Office. Photo Credit: UpstateNYer Chief Copyright Royalty Judge Trevor Jefferson recently issued that noteworthy order, calling on the major labels, the A2IM, the Music Artists Coalition, the NMPA, and the NSAI to respond to objections and standalone questions about their Phono V agreement. Those parties in late June moved to finalize said proposed Phono V settlement, which, if approved, would set mechanical rates for physical formats, permanent downloads, ringtones, and bundles between 2028 and 2032. But as many already know from our exclusive coverage, the terms at hand elicited considerable pushback – including from Word Collections, the Songwriters Guild of America (SGA), activist songwriter George Johnson, Eminem publisher Eight Mile Style, and the Society of Composers & Lyricists (SCL). And it’s this pushback, pertaining to the “demonstrably unreasonable” proposed Phono V settlement’s reversion to a 12-cent “reset rate” (down from 13.1 cents at present) and more, that prompted the CRB to request further information. Here, the CRB pointed to the SCL’s concerns about a conflict of interest between the settling parties; the SGA’s and Word Collections’ above-highlighted rate-reset and inflation-data arguments; and Eight Mile’s criticism of the ringtone-rate freeze. Now, the majors, the NMPA, the NSAI, and the other settling entities have until October 2nd to formally address these objections. Just as – or perhaps more – interestingly, the CRB ordered the same parties to submit “specific enumerated answers” to 10 standalone questions. “Does the settlement include a mechanical base rate of 12 cents? If so, why is it reasonable for the mechanical floor rate to not track increases in the CPI-U?” the clear-cut opening query reads. Additionally, “one or more of the Judges” asked the settling parties to clarify, if applicable, why this 12-cent rate is “still being applied”; whether the underlying cost-of-living adjustment factors for CPI shifts during the highly inflationary 2021-22 window; what the base rate would be if said shifts were incorporated into the calculations; and “why it would be economically accurate to omit the CPI-U increases for 2021 and 2022 in the settlement rates for the Phonorecords V period.” Without jumping to conclusions based on the questions’ tone and substance, it seems safe to describe the inquiries as indicative of possibly far-reaching Phono V settlement scrutiny from the CRB. And if there is ownership overlap, the relevant participants should “describe that relationship in a manner that reflects the extent of either separateness or combination between them sufficient to demonstrate that the settlement agreement was nonetheless an arm’s-length transaction,” per the order. “Are there documents, including negotiation documents, emails, or other materials, evidencing the corporate separateness or common ownership across the Movants that the Movants would voluntarily provide to the Judges for their review that would demonstrate the settlement reflects an arm’s-length negotiation between willing sellers (licensors) and willing buyers (licensees)?” the ninth question reads in part. Finally, the last question centers on the settlement-talks participation (or lack thereof) of the objectors; previously, Word Collections and the SGA, despite having “attempted to convey on numerous occasions” their willingness to engage in constructive Phono V discussions, described their contact with the settling parties as “extremely limited.” More immediately, the CRB also bifurcated the current Phono V proceeding from its streaming counterpart and stayed the process (regarding physical, download, and ringtone rates, that is) “until further notice.” In a statement, Songwriters Guild of America President Rick Carnes applauded the CRB’s order and reiterated his organization’s desire to achieve a deal benefiting “all parties.” “We are simply looking for a deal negotiated at arm’s length that benefits all parties, including America’s independent music creators, who deserve transparency, clarity, and a strong voice in negotiating fair rates of remuneration for the use of their copyrighted works,” Carnes said. “We now have great hope that the CRB judges share that vision in the Phonorecords V proceeding, and have taken action to better ensure such equitable results.”

title: Fathom's 20th-anniversary rerelease of V For Vendetta gets a new trailer - avclub.com
content: Here’s tough news for folks old enough to have seen James McTeigue’s R-rated adaptation of Alan Moore and David Lloyd’s V For Vendetta in theaters: Fathom Entertainment has announced that tickets are now available for the film’s 20th-anniversary rerelease at participating theaters and has released a new trailer to mark the occasion. The new screenings, slated for November 1 and (appropriately enough) 5, will feature Freedom Forever, an exclusive featurette with McTeigue, who discusses the making of the 2006 film and how its anti-authoritarian message still resonates today. Fathom’s Vice President of Marketing Shannah Miller said in a statement, “The award-winning V For Vendetta graphic novel led to one of the most provocative films in the early 2000s. Twenty years later, V For Vendetta still asks the questions that matter: About freedom, identity, and who gets to speak up. Fathom is thrilled to bring this great movie back to theatres, featuring an exclusive new conversation with director James McTeigue for a whole new generation of audiences.” Reviewing for The A.V. Club in 2006, Keith Phipps said the Natalie Portman and Hugo Weaving film was “a compelling, visually striking political mystery with some big ideas woven into it—subversive notions about integrity, liberty, and political change. And though it stutters in getting it out, the film clearly means what it says.” The trailer features new music from Jonathan Snipes of the experimental hip-hop group clipping, who offers a sugary take on Tchaikovsky’s 1812 Overture (a dramatically important piece of music in the film), a quirky, glitchy, squiggly piece that only partially undercuts the oomph of the movie’s imagery. But then, we’re not trailer editors, so don’t take our word for it. You can watch the trailer below. Maybe, in the original Once Upon A Time… In Hollywood, Cliff Booth was never as famous as Rick Dalton. But based on the new trailer for its sequel The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth, which Netflix released this morning, he’s achieved a new level of infamy, presumably partially inspired by the events at the end of the first film. But when we meet him, he’s laying fairly low, working and running at a movie theater, John Wilson style. The official, long synopsis for Cliff Booth reads: Murder, blackmail, theft, extortion — just another summer in Hollywood. It’s 1977, eight years since Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt) encountered the Manson family in Quentin Tarantino’s parallel history of 1969, Once Upon A Time… In Hollywood. In THE FURTHER MIS-ADVENTURES OF CLIFF BOOTH, directed by David Fincher from a new script by Tarantino, the fairytale is over. Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s greats and, sometimes, not so good. He’s curious when he gets a call from talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), on behalf of her client, TV megastar Charlie Peters (Scott Caan) — a man known for doing his own stunts. And he’s further entertained and intrigued when he meets other characters in Charlie’s world, from his knowing wife Toni (Carla Gugino) to pro football champion turned screen star Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). Then there are the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), mysterious gangsters causing mayhem across the city. What was once a fairytale is now a crime story — a cocktail of violence, ambition, and desire that could only happen in LA. The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth opens in IMAX theaters on November 25 before coming to Netflix on December 23. Succession actor Jeremy Strong’s commitment to The Method is well documented at this point (even one of his more traditional costars hasn’t got much patience for the practice.) But according to Aaron Sorkin, Strong’s dedication to staying in character as Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg made him—hold on to your hats—not that much fun to be around on the set of The Social Reckoning. “[Jeremy] did not speak in his own voice on the set or walk the way Jeremy walks,” Sorkin, writer-director of the long-awaited sequel 2010’s The Social Network told the New York Times‘ The Interview. As reported by Deadline, Sorkin explained to other actors in the upcoming film about the fallout from a 2021 Wall Street Journal expose of Facebook, “I told all the other actors in his scenes: ‘Guys, he’s not going to be hanging out with you at craft service. He’s not going to be yucking it up with you between takes. He’s probably not going to speak to you at all,'” adding ominously, “‘He is going to treat you the way he imagines Mark treats the people around him.'” The infamously awkward tech billionaire was notably played to twitchy, dead-eyed perfection by Oscar-nominated Jesse Eisenberg in the first film, while Strong, no stranger to imbuing characters with an eerie sense of unspoken inner weirdness, will take over for the sequel. Still, Strong’s assiduous nature when it comes to his work saw him surprise Sorkin by penning a letter to Zuckerberg before filming, promising that he would portray the controversial CEO “with respect.” That being established, trailers for the film, which releases in theaters on October 9, do see Strong’s iteration of Zuckerberg bristling with pent-up billionaire’s fury that former Facebook employee Frances Haugen (played by Anora‘s Mikey Madison) would dare expose the ongoing harm his social network is causing to users by amplifying hate speech to increase engagement. “The debate is over,” Strong’s creepily accurate Zuckerberg snaps at one objection, in between sessions of being taught how to nod like a human being. Practically any time another celebrity speaks of former Happy Days icon Henry Winkler, the phrase, “nicest guy in the world,” comes up. But Winkler, whose late-career resurgence has seen the actor rack up accolades for his roles in Barry and Arrested Development among others, is still a human being. A human being with a few grudges, as it turns out. As reported by Variety, in a revealing recent interview on the podcast In Depth With Graham Bensinger, the 80-year-old actor raised a few eyebrows by discussing his decades-long friction with fellow Hollywood nice guy Tom Hanks (Turner & Hooch is still doing damage, people), and further dished on the lingering resentment he has with the producers of Scream. (He did warm hearts by noting how he and director Wes Craven would have sushi together all the time.) Calling his anecdote about his time playing doomed Principal Arthur Himbry in Craven’s influential slasher “a parable for anybody who wants to be an actor,” Winkler told his host about his disillusioning brush with the film’s marketing department. “The studio comes to me and says, ‘We can’t put your name on the film. We cannot put you anywhere near the poster,'” Winkler reports, noting that execs cited his time as Happy Days‘ Arthur “The Fonz” Fonzarelli would “knock the balance of horror off” if people saw Winkler’s face on the film’s poster. Winkler, benevolent bringer of cakes to film crews everywhere according to Barry costar Bill Hader, is still an actor with some pride, as evidenced by his confession that he was “bewildered,” “upset” and “insulted” by the slight at the time. Naturally, noted mensch Winkler then agreed to then do press for the film due to his allegiance to the people he’d worked with (most of whom got their mugs on all the advertising.) As Winkler concluded the parable in signature wise uncle mode, “You just show up. You have no idea what’s going to happen, but that’s out of your control.” And while it had been some 12 years at that point since Happy Days ended its run, maybe the universally beloved actor can take solace in the fact that his then most famous character loomed large enough to rob him of some marquee face time.

title: Coen discusses key area where Jaguars faltered in Week 2 loss v. Broncos - Yahoo Sports
content: It was a quiet day for the Jacksonville Jaguars' pass rush in the team's Week 2 matchup against the Denver Broncos. According to PFF, the Jaguars totaled just 11 pressures on the day. No Jaguars player had more than two quarterback pressures and, as a team, Jacksonville didn't record a single sack. Broncos' quarterback Bo Nix was under pressure on just 31.3% of his dropbacks, which ranks 23rd out of 31 eligible quarterbacks with the Monday Night Football game still to take place. Even when the Jaguars blitzed, the Broncos seemed to often have the answers. Denver does have a stout offensive line unit, but as head coach Liam Coen said afterward, the Jaguars are going to have to find a way to create pressure against good teams. "That [Denver] is a damn good offensive line," Coen said afterward, via Jaguars.com. "I don't want to take too much away from them, but if we're going to beat a team like that, then we're going to have to create some pressure. They caught us in a couple blitzes that they identified pre-snap when we were going to blitz and bring more. They ended up flipping the protections to pick some of that stuff up. That's something we have to look at as well in terms of when we're bringing pressure. If they identify it, hey, can we get out of it, or whatever it is. When we do blitz, we got to get home." With Nix having time in the pocket, he and the Denver passing game were able to generate a number of explosive plays through the air. While there was certainly good from the Jaguars' defense in this game, those positives were negated by the Broncos' big plays, which often led to points. The pass rush depth for the Jaguars was a big question mark coming into the season, and while those doubts were quieted after Week 1, they may now be back heading into Week 3. title: The Trojan Horse Rides Again: On the Swedish Supreme Court’s MFN Ruling in Okuashvili v. Georgia - Wolters Kluwer
content: The Trojan Horse Rides Again: On the Swedish Supreme Court’s MFN Ruling in Okuashvili v. Georgia On 26 June 2026, Sweden’s Supreme Court (“Court”) handed down judgment in Zaza Okuashvili v. Georgia, reversing the Svea Court of Appeal’s judgment and holding that an SCC tribunal could take jurisdiction over a claim against Georgia by combining the most-favored-nation (“MFN”) clause of one treaty with the dispute settlement clause of an entirely different one. The MFN clause’s capacity to reach into dispute settlement has often been described as a Trojan Horse, since contracting parties introduce the clause themselves. The Court has given the horse free rein by allowing an investor to switch arbitral forums via an MFN clause. This post makes two arguments: first, that the Court widened the MFN clause’s scope beyond the limits recognized by previous tribunals; second, that it failed to give due weight to the contextual requirement of State consent, overlooking considerations mandated by Articles 31 and 32 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (“VCLT”). The facts of the case and the Court’s reasoning are set out in a previous Blog post in full (see here), this piece confines itself to two specific respects in which that reasoning falls short. Okuashvili holds both Georgian and British nationality (¶4). Due to Article 25(2)(a) of the ICSID Convention, Okuashvili was barred from arbitrating against his own State “regardless of what other citizenship he or she holds,” and this dual nationality excluded him from Article 8 of the UK-Georgia BIT that only offers ICSID arbitration (¶1, ¶5). The BIT’s MFN clause, Article 3, explicitly extends to Article 1 to 11 (¶2). Georgia’s separate treaty with the Belgo-Luxembourg Economic Union (“BLEU”) lets investors choose among ICSID, the ICC, or the SCC (¶3). Okuashvili used the MFN clause to reach into the BLEU treaty’s more permissive forum and commenced SCC arbitration against Georgia (¶6). The tribunal accepted jurisdiction; however, the Svea Court of Appeal set aside the award (¶7). The Court has now reinstated the tribunal’s approach (¶¶60-62). The intervening procedural history is set out in the previous Blog post referenced above. Two findings of the Court are of importance. The Court held that ICSID and SCC arbitration are “of the same kind” under the ejusdem generis principle, since both are “established arbitration dispute resolution mechanisms” (¶46). It acknowledged that Article 8 reflects the “preferred” ICSID-exclusive version of the UK’s 1991 model investment treaty, deliberately chosen over a version offering investors a choice of fora – yet held that this choice “cannot be given any decisive importance” (¶47). Whether an MFN clause can reach a treaty’s dispute-settlement machinery has been debated for decades. The question was already argued in the 1950s, in the Ambatielos arbitration between Greece and the United Kingdom, where the ICJ confirmed the relevance of the ejusdem generis rule but dismissed the claim on its merits for failing to show any “privileges, favours or immunities… more extensive than those resulting from the basic treaty.” It was Maffezini v. Spain that first used MFN as a weapon to create jurisdiction. The tribunal let an investor skip an eighteen-month local-litigation requirement under the Argentina-Spain BIT by importing a more permissive dispute-settlement clause from Spain’s treaty with Chile, reasoning that dispute settlement is “inextricably related” to investment protection and therefore falls within the clause’s reach (¶¶54-56). Siemens v. Argentina and Gas Natural v. Argentina followed suit, apparently settling the question in the investor’s favour. However, other tribunals placed limitations on this rule. Plama v. Bulgaria and Salini v. Jordan held that an MFN clause cannot import dispute-settlement provisions “unless [it] leaves no doubt that the contracting parties intended to incorporate them” (Plama, ¶223). Wintershall v. Argentina’s stricter interpretation stated that an MFN clause cannot extend to procedural provisions without clear and unambiguous language. By 2015 the split had become pronounced enough that the International Law Commission’s Study Group devoted its entire final report to the MFN clause, concluding that tribunals would keep deciding the question case by case – not exactly the clear boundary needed. (¶216). Two features of Maffezini’s own reasoning are directly relevant here and were overlooked by the Court entirely. The Maffezini tribunal, while expanding the MFN clause to dispute resolution, warned of the consequences and signaled that the clause’s scope should be narrowly construed. It held that the beneficiary of the clause should not be able to override fundamental conditions for acceptance of the agreement, especially if the beneficiary is the private investor (¶62). The tribunal listed the most prominent situations where the clause should not apply, including where “the agreement provides for a particular arbitration forum, such as ICSID, this option cannot be changed by invoking the clause, in order to refer the dispute to a different system of arbitration” (¶63). Okuashvili does swap ICSID for SCC arbitration, precisely what the Maffezini tribunal anticipated and excluded. Plama and Salini confronted investors making this exact move and rejected it. In Plama, the tribunal refused to let a Bulgaria-Cyprus dispute travel from ad hoc arbitration into ICSID arbitration through the MFN clause, applying the “no doubt” standard quoted above (¶223). Salini reached the same conclusion on comparable facts (¶¶102–19). One case might support the Supreme Court’s conclusion: Garanti Koza v. Turkmenistan where the tribunal substituted an exclusive ICSID arbitration clause with another BIT’s dispute resolution clause that gave investors the option between ICSID and UNCITRAL. But that case drew heavy criticism for manufacturing consent the underlying treaty never gave. None of this appears in the Swedish judgment. Instead, the Court works around the exceptions by finding that ICSID and SCC arbitration are “of the same kind” for ejusdem generis purposes, since both are established institutional forms of arbitration (¶46). This observation, while true, answers the wrong question. The forum-substitution exception has nothing to do with how institutions resemble each other; it has to do with whether a particular forum was the price of a State’s consent. Two arbitral institutions can be equally similar, and it will still be true that a State agreed to be sued in one of them and not the other. The extension of an MFN clause may be defensible where it removes an objectively burdensome procedural obligation that places an investor in a less favorable position than investors protected under comparable third-party treaties. The same justification, however, does not extend to investors seeking merely to substitute one arbitral forum for another based on their own interests. The second problem lies in how the Court read the treaty’s drafting history. The Court acknowledged that the UK offered two dispute-settlement templates in its 1991 model investment treaty: an ICSID exclusive “preferred” version, and a “alternative” version letting investors choose among ICSID, the ICC, and ad hoc arbitration (¶47). Georgia and the UK chose the exclusive one. A significant number of UK BITs concluded before 1991 used a single forum by default and the rationale behind introducing a broader template was to let treaty partners decide. Choosing between two available options is a form of expression, and arguably a more reliable one than the text of either option read in isolation, since it shows what the parties considered and rejected as well as what they accepted. The Court rightfully identified that this question should be answered under Articles 31 and 32 of the VCLT. Article 31(1) of the VCLT treats this kind of surrounding practice as part of a treaty’s context. Article 32’s reference to the circumstances of a treaty’s conclusion points the same way. The Court weighs it for exactly one sentence, concluding that the UK’s alternative version “cannot be given any decisive importance in the interpretation,” without elaborating on why this is so. The irony is that the Court had already committed itself to the opposite principle elsewhere in the same judgment invoking  effet utile - the idea that a treaty should be interpreted to avoid redundancy - to justify reading the MFN clause broadly (¶16). But effet utile cuts both ways. If the ICSID-exclusive template can be undone by a later MFN clause, then the “preferred” and “alternative” versions of the UK Model BIT lose their difference: whichever one a State signs, an investor can reach the other anyway. That is not giving effect to the treaty’s drafting choices. This does not mean that MFN clauses should be shut out of dispute settlement. The holdings of previous tribunals, on procedural preconditions, remain sound. The objection here is narrower, and for that reason harder to wave away: on the specific question of substituting one arbitral forum for another, the Court has misapplied the one boundary that was set for that exact maneuver and treated a State’s considered choice between two negotiating templates as though it carried no interpretive weight whatsoever. The case now goes back to the Svea Court of Appeal on a narrow remand (¶61). Whatever that court does with it, other tribunals reading this judgment for guidance on the MFN question would do well to treat it as an outlier rather than a template. ©2025 Wolters Kluwer N.V. and/or its subsidiaries. The house always wins — but now the house has some serious competition, and that's triggered an explosion of shock marketing and promotions in the sports betting space. Why it matters: DraftKings and FanDuel — and a few smaller sportsbooks — had largely cornered the sports gambling industry until prediction markets suddenly began threatening their turf. The big picture: Kalshi, Polymarket and upstarts like Novig have been signing celebrity sponsors and airing splashy ads this football season in a stark reflection of the intensifying competition for wagers. Ad spending by prediction markets and the major sportsbooks rose 21% in the first seven months of 2026, compared to the same period a year earlier, according to Nielsen research provided to Axios. State of play: A slew of new celebrity sponsor deals illustrate the rising marketing power of prediction markets. In sports, LeBron James, Derek Jeter and Eli Manning signed deals with Polymarket, while Giannis Antetokounmpo joined Kalshi. In entertainment, Spike Lee and Alexandra Daddario have done ads for Polymarket, while Timothée Chalamet has appeared in ads for Kalshi. Perhaps most notably, actress Sydney Sweeney drew an avalanche of attention to little-known prediction market Novig this month with ads in which she's wearing little to no clothing. The Sweeney ads — like her controversial American Eagle campaign in 2025 — sparked a backlash over their salaciousness. Follow the money: The latest ad blitz shows that prediction markets realize the football season is a crucial period for betting in the U.S., says Dustin Gouker, a gambling industry analyst. "The start of the football season has always been the best time to acquire customers for sports betting, no matter what is going on in the world," Gouker tells Axios. But now "the map has expanded." State of Play: Traditional sportsbooks had about 76% of legal U.S. sports wagering in 2023, but that share fell to 64% in the first half of 2026, according to research by digital market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Prediction markets went from 1% to 16% during that period. The impact: For the conventional sportsbooks, the upshot is a more promotional environment that's forcing many of them to offer profit boosts, bonus bets and better rewards to attract customers. At sportsbook Bet365, for example, some customers effectively received a free $50 for placing a bet on teams to score any points in an NFL game. At Flutter Entertainment, which owns FanDuel, the company expects to take a $270 million hit in adjusted earnings as it invests in its U.S. sportsbook. CFO Robert Coldrake on a recent earnings call described it as "an investment in generosity spend." Yes, but: DraftKings, FanDuel and Fanatics have their own prediction markets that allow them to compete with Kalshi and Polymarket in states where online gambling hasn't been legalized. When you open the DraftKings app now, it says "now live in all 50 states," even though the sportsbook side and prediction markets product operate under entirely different legal frameworks. What we're watching: The marketing boom could come crashing down if the prediction markets lose their legal bid to maintain operations in the states that are challenging their authority to operate. Legal experts widely expect the U.S. Supreme Court to take up the case over whether prediction markets should be regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission or by state gaming commissions. The prediction markets say "event contracts" are properly regulated at the federal level. Critics say it's gambling under a different name. "Whether you call it sports betting or sports trading, sports markets are now available in all 50 states, and it does seem like that is here to stay," Novig CEO Jacob Fortinsky told Axios in an unpublished interview earlier this year. The bottom line: The prediction market ad blitz bears a resemblance to the sportsbook commercials that dominated the airwaves in the years after the Supreme Court opened the door to legalized gambling in 2018. title: Was Hawthorn v Brisbane the best game of Australian rules football ever played? | Jonathan Horn - The Guardian
content: This preliminary final showcased everything that is exquisite, brutal and cruel about the sport. And how about Nick Watson? Some of the most memorable games in the history of Australian rules football have come in preliminary finals. Some, like Geelong’s win over North Melbourne in 1994, are remembered as wildly fluctuating, end-to-end shootouts. Some, like Collingwood v GWS in 2023, were hand-to-hand combat. Some, like Hawthorn’s win over Melbourne in 1987 and Sydney’s over Essendon in 1996, are remembered for their dramatic finishes. Some, like the Crows-Bulldogs game in 1997, wrenched the hearts out of the losing supporters. Some are remembered for individual brilliance – Ablett in 1989, Long in 1993, Kouta in 1999 and Cox in 2018. And some, like the 2016 prelim in western Sydney and the Brisbane-Geelong game in 2024, are remembered for the high standard of play throughout. The Brisbane-Hawthorn prelim on Saturday sampled the best of those and distilled them into one discombobulating, unforgettable brew. It had violent momentum swings, exceptional skills, tactical intrigue and plenty of controversy. And that was just the opening 20 minutes. One of our greatest historians once called Australian football an “emotional bath of agony and ecstasy”. Hyperbole butters a lot of bread in footy. But if ever that phrase was applicable, it was this game. It might be the greatest of all the preliminary finals. It might be the finest exhibition of the code we’ve ever seen. It’s hard to know where to begin with a game like that, so I may as well start with the ending – Sam Mitchell’s press conference. He tumbled into the presser with the enthusiasm of a man about to undergo root canal surgery. “This feeling is the pits,” he said. It’s good to see a coach in pieces like that – no spin, no “learnings”, no next week. He spoke of rage, desolation, confusion, pride. His team certainly had a lot to be proud of. They’d climbed off the canvas. They’d fallen 28 points behind one of the best teams we’ve ever seen. They’d been tromped on at centre stoppages. But they never yielded. They rattled home. They had one hand on a grand final berth, until the hairy hand of football intervened. It’s also worth touching on the free kick against Jarman Impey. The cojones on that umpire to make that call cannot be underestimated. With a baying crowd, a season on the line, and seconds on the clock, he put himself in the right spot and he didn’t flinch. Impey was tackled, his arm was free, and he didn’t get rid of the ball properly. Yes, there were some line-ball decisions all day, and in the final minutes in particular. But that was a gutsy call, and he should be commended, not pelted with bottles. At various stages, both sides bent, but did not break. Initially, it was the Lions who lurched back to life. They were 22 points down. They were being torched by Nick Watson. They didn’t have a natural match up for him. But who the hell does? They were being well beaten by a team playing sublime football. We said something similar in last year’s preliminary final. They hit Collingwood with two quick jabs after half-time and the whole mood of the ground, game and season shifted. This year’s turnaround didn’t have the immediate shock value of that. It was more gradual, more structural. But 10 minutes into the third quarter and it was abundantly clear – this was Brisbane’s game now. It was at their tempo, on their terms, in their house. As Mitchell later said, there was a point where he wondered whether his Hawks simply weren’t good enough. But Brisbane lowered their gloves and Hawthorn seized the initiative. Mitchell says Josh Ward is the only player who could win two most improved player trophies in as many years, and he tilted the contest in the final quarter. And then there was Watson. Every time he did something preposterous, Chris Fagan had the bewildered look of a man who knew there wasn’t a player in Australia who could have done anything about it. His fifth goal might have been his best, when he appeared off the grid like an apparition to toe it through. He is a startling footballer, and Fremantle would be counting their lucky stars they don’t have to worry about him this week. Some of the heroics earlier in the game – Conor McKenna’s Gaelic conjuring job and Charlie Cameron thwacking a goal in front of the members stand – feel like they happened a month ago. And even the mayhem of the final few minutes were a jangle of moments that may get lost in the wash – Tom Barrass’s mark, Impey’s rundown tackle on McKenna, Brisbane’s gang tackling on the last line of defence, Mitch Lewis’s horizontal launch, Levi Ashcroft’s lunging spoil, and the oceanic calm of his brother Will as he skipped out of that final stoppage. Josh Dunkley had three or four interventions at the end that shifted the trajectory of play – a block here, a fist there. He said afterwards it was the most emotionally and physically demanding game he’s played in since the 2016 preliminary final. An argument could be made that they’re the two best games we’ve ever seen, and he was magnificent in both of them. This final showcased everything that is exquisite, exhilarating, brutal and cruel about the sport. It’s a game that will be talked about for generations to come. title: Archie Weatherspoon V Commits as Cal Poly Men's Basketball's Top Recruit Ever - Mustang News

Cal Poly Men’s Basketball has officially landed its highest-rated recruit in program history in combo guard Archie Weatherspoon V. Weatherspoon V, who attends Rangeview High School in Aurora, Colo., announced on Sunday that he plans to join the Mustangs next season. Weatherspoon V is a three-star recruit according to 247Sports and is ranked the 247th player in the country and the third-highest in the state of Colorado. The 6-foot-3 guard held offers from programs such as Cal, Creighton, UNLV and High Point but ultimately opted to join Head Coach Mike DeGeorge and the Mustangs. With a 247Sports composite rating of .8950, Weatherspoon V surpasses Brantly Stevenson (2020) as the outlet’s highest-ranked Cal Poly recruit in history. DeGeorge’s previous coaching stint at Colorado Mesa gave him familiarity with Weatherspoon V’s home state, a potential advantage while recruiting against higher-profile programs. Weatherspoon V profiles as a potential lead guard while remaining a high-level scoring threat, using his 6-foot-8 wingspan to slice through defenses and get to the basket. Weatherspoon V has been highly efficient at the high school level and possesses a clean, repeatable shooting form. Weatherspoon V averaged 19.2 points, 4.0 rebounds, 3.7 assists and 1.6 steals per game across 26 games in his junior season. title: The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that | Editorial - The Guardian
content: OpenAI claims its agents have solved the Navier-Stokes problem. But questions remain about how useful and independent its work really is On 8 September, OpenAI claimed that its AI agents had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the most famous and difficult challenges in mathematics. Had a human solved it, they would have collected both prize money and plaudits from their fellows. The announcement instead ignited what some mathematicians have called an “existential crisis” in their field over the power of AI, and accusations that OpenAI misused human work. The maths behind Navier-Stokes is difficult to understand, but the critiques levelled by mathematicians will be familiar to artists, office workers, or anyone else concerned about AI. OpenAI’s results, like any arising from a large language model, depend on digesting work by human mathematicians. The OpenAI paper cites sources, but many believe the company didn’t give sufficient credit, especially to several mathematicians believed to be very close to a solution – bad form that erases human ingenuity and hogs all the glory. The mathematician Tristan Buckmaster also has concerns that work he was doing on Navier-Stokes using OpenAI’s Codex model was seen by the OpenAI team. OpenAI has denied directly accessing this material, but could not rule out that data from Buckmaster’s use of their products “helped improve our model”. This lack of attribution and compensation for the human labour that AI is built on has turned many against the companies that develop these systems. It has yet to be adequately addressed. This is a particular misstep in the case of mathematics. As many mathematicians have pointed out, AI firms are keen to use their models’ maths prowess as an advertisement. But they rely on mathematicians to check their – often sloppy and baffling – work, and to tell them if it is useful and how it might be applied. An AI-produced movie or vaccine would have a clear and obvious use, whatever its merits, but it will take time and human intellectual labour to tell whether OpenAI’s purported solution contains any novel mathematical tools or insights. This should be an opportunity for collaboration. It has instead become yet another source of alienation and resentment. Despite this, mathematicians are remarkably open to the use of AI, even as they commit their names to open letters denouncing tech firms. Most recognise that the technology is undeniably powerful and particularly good at maths. There has been a nuanced discussion of how maths might change and integrate AI, with humans guiding and interpreting its work. There has also been some soul-searching as to whether celebrating the person – or machine – that achieved a flashy final result in the form of a mathematical proof is the best way to value contributions. As Bill Thurston, the Fields Medal-winning mathematician, put it in 2010, well before the age of AI: “The product of mathematics is clarity and understanding. Not theorems, by themselves.” These are still uniquely human qualities. Some critics of AI are still stuck dismissing its outputs as uniformly useless “slop”. AI will not become good at everything. But more people may find themselves in the current position of mathematicians, confronted with the undeniable effectiveness of AI, while deeply concerned about how it is being used. This anxiety might not exist, the mathematician Nestor Guillen wrote recently, if we could separate the tech from the tech companies, and democratise its use. It is increasingly urgent that we find ways to do so.

title: CR-V Laps The RAV4, And Honda Isn't Coasting - thetruthaboutcars.com
content: Toyota's all-new, all-hybrid RAV4 was supposed to spend 2026 doing what the RAV4 always does: sit near the top of the sales charts as the best-selling thing in America that isn't an F-Series. Fresh styling, more power, better efficiency. Instead, production problems knocked sales down early in the year, and the Honda CR-V walked right through the open door. Honda's lead is now large enough that Toyota probably can't reel it back before the calendar runs out. Rather than sit on that advantage, Honda appears to be pressing it. According to Japanese outlet Nikkei, production of a new-generation CR-V hybrid starts in Canada in February, with the Indiana and Ohio plants following in March. That points to cars reaching dealers before summer, sooner than the previously expected late-2026 window. That's a quick turnaround for a model that's only been on sale since the 2023 model year. The changes run deep. Honda's compact and midsize hybrid family — Civic, CR-V, and Accord — has been in line for a reworked architecture and drivetrain, previewed by a running prototype late last year. The new chassis is lighter and reportedly up to 10 percent cheaper to build. The powertrain keeps a naturally aspirated 2.0-liter four but adds direct injection and new electric motors for efficiency. Honda is also porting over the Prelude's simulated shifting, some power-control tricks meant to aid handling, and reportedly a sportier exhaust note. The RAV4 may well recover once Toyota gets production back to full pace. But a cheaper, more efficient CR-V isn't the only thing waiting for it. Beginning of dialog window. Notably, both Honda and Nissan are prioritizing the hybrid variants. With gas prices spiking, that timing looks less like a coincidence and more like where the segment is heading.
