title: The Only Manual, V8, Rear-Wheel Drive Sedan Left In The USA Now Produces 685 HP - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update The golden age of the V8 performance sedan felt like it would last forever — a supercharged engine up front, three pedals on the floor, five seats, and power routed strictly to the rear wheels. That formula produced some of the most celebrated driver's cars ever made, and for a while, the options were plentiful. Today, the market has moved on almost entirely. Electrification, all-wheel drive, and turbocharged six-cylinders have replaced the old recipe — almost. In 2026, exactly one sedan on sale in the United States still checks every box: the Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing. By now, you know the CT5-V Blackwing's headline figures, with the supercharged 6.2-liter V8 pumping out a thunderous 668 horsepower and 659 lb-ft of torque. While the BMW M5 and performance sedans of its ilk have paired that much power with AWD for the better part of a decade, Cadillac's refusal to drive the front axle is admirable. But making the manual standard? That's worthy of a parade through the streets. The manual is a six-speed unit sourced from transmission specialists Tremec, featuring No-Lift Shift functionality and Active Rev-Matching for the most performance possible from a car with three pedals. With one of the most beautifully balanced chassis, a long wheelbase, keen steering, and the ability to row gears yourself, the CT5-V Blackwing makes a strong case for being crowned one of the best performance sedans ever built. The only problem is that this has officially been declared the final send-off for the ICE-powered Cadillac V-Series, and while the manual was retained for the facelift (thanks to a nearly 50 percent take rate for the six-speed in 2023), when the CT5-V Blackwing thunders off into the night, it'll take that six-speed with it. For 2026, Cadillac introduced the CT5-V Blackwing F1 Collector Series, celebrating the brand's first Grand Prix in the USA. It's not a phone-in special edition, either. In addition to distinctive design features, Cadillac fitted a new supercharger that lifts output to 685 hp and 673 lb-ft of torque. Only 26 will be built, and it's virtually guaranteed to appreciate in value. The standard car is already the last of its kind — this is by far the most extreme version of it. People like to hype current models as future classics to artificially inflate their values, but the CT5-V Blackwing might actually have a genuine case. The F1 Collector Series says it right in the name — it's a special variant with more power than the already-impressive standard car, courtesy of a new supercharger, and such a limited production run is sure to drive up values. Setting the rare variant aside, the standard Blackwing holds its value better than most cars. In fact, the debut model year's base MSRP in 2022 was $83,995, and used examples have retained a remarkable share of that figure — only a roughly 10% drop in four years, whereas many other cars lose half their value in a similar timeframe through normal depreciation. Buyers are spending even more on special variants, like the First Edition Series from 2022 (250 units produced) or the 2023 model year's 120-year Anniversary Edition, of which 120 units were produced. We're confident the latest F1 Collector Series will command serious attention at future auctions. While current CT5 production ends in late 2026, General Motors has officially greenlit a second-generation CT5 platform, and reports indicate a next-generation CT5-V Blackwing successor will follow, but nothing has been confirmed. Built on an updated Alpha architecture, the incoming internal combustion luxury sedan is expected to arrive for the 2027 or 2028 model year. While Cadillac has re-evaluated its all-electric timeline, precise powertrain details remain under wraps. Enthusiasts are watching closely to see if GM retains a supercharged V8 and six-speed manual option, or pivots toward a high-output forced-induction or hybrid setup to keep America's ultimate performance sedan alive. Over the last five years, the American automotive industry has undergone a quiet execution of the V8 performance sedan. A segment that once epitomized effortless highway cruising and tire-shredding muscle has been systematically dismantled by tightening emissions mandates, downsizing, and forced induction. Major high-volume staples like the Dodge Charger R/T, Scat Pack, and Hellcat variants—alongside its understated luxury sibling, the Chrysler 300C—were officially retired, taking the legendary Hemi V8 platform down with them. Luxury benchmarks were not spared either; Cadillac dropped the twin-turbo Blackwing V8 in the short-lived CT6-V, leaving only the hand-built, supercharged 6.2-liter CT5-V Blackwing to carry the mantle for domestic four-doors. Beyond Detroit, foreign alternatives like the naturally aspirated Lexus IS 500 F Sport and Mercedes-AMG’s V8 C63 have either bowed out or downsized to complex hybrid setups. Today, the once-flourishing V8 sedan market is reduced to a handful of expensive, low-volume holdouts, shifting real V8 enthusiast demand straight to the pre-owned market. It's fitting for Cadillac to be the last bastion of the rear-wheel-drive V8 sedan, since the automaker has offered so many compelling options throughout its history. Some of its more recent sports sedans — the current CT5-V and CT4-V — use turbocharged six- and four-cylinder engines, respectively. For genuine V8 models, you have to look further back. An often overlooked and increasingly rare example is the STS-V. Sold from the 2006 through 2009 model years, it was powered by a 4.4-liter supercharged V8 producing 469 horsepower and 439 lb-ft of torque. It's not worth much today, having been overshadowed by the less-powerful but more celebrated CTS-V sedan from the same era. While the STS-V lasted only a single generation, the CTS-V went on to achieve genuine icon status, eventually spanning sedan, coupe, and wagon variants. A more modern — and similarly overlooked — model that some readers may not even know about is Cadillac's CT6-V. The CT6 launched for the 2016 model year, and its V-Series variant arrived for just two model years, 2019 and 2020. Under the hood sat a 4.2-liter twin-turbo V8 making 550 hp and 640 lb-ft of torque, sent to the rear wheels through a 10-speed automatic. The 0–60 mph sprint took under four seconds.
